summary: An island nation in the South Pacific made up of more than eighty islands, formerly an Anglo-French condominium, independent in 1980, and one of the countries with the highest language density in the world.

ranking.name: Presbyterian Church
ranking.description: In 1839 the London Missionary Society missionary John Williams was killed when he landed on Erromango, showing the difficulty of early missionary work. In 1848 John Geddie, a Presbyterian missionary from Nova Scotia, Canada, founded a mission station on Aneityum in the south, after which the Presbyterians preached on a large scale on the southern and central islands and ran schools. The Presbyterian church trained many leaders of the independence movement and politics, and so became the largest denomination.

ranking.name: Anglican Church
ranking.description: The Anglican "Melanesian Mission" was founded from 1849 by the New Zealand bishop Selwyn, with the northern islands as its main field, and trained local evangelists. When Vanuatu became independent in 1980, its first prime minister, Walter Lini, was an Anglican priest, giving the Anglican church an important place in the process of nation-building; its followers are concentrated mainly in the north.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church arrived in Vanuatu in the early 20th century and attracted followers through running schools, medical services and promoting healthy living (such as avoiding pork and alcohol). Because it requires giving up some traditional customs, it also creates tension with local culture, but its membership has grown steadily, making it the third-largest denomination.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Marist missionaries of the Catholic Church came to Vanuatu in 1887. During the joint Anglo-French administration of the New Hebrides from 1906 to 1980, the French side supported the Catholic church in running French-language schools, so Catholics are often associated with a French-language educational background. Around independence, the political divide between the French-speaking and English-speaking areas also partly overlapped with the distinction between Catholics and Protestants.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs (including the John Frum movement, etc.)
ranking.description: Traditional belief (locally called "kastom") values ancestors, land and tribal rituals, and is still fully preserved on some islands. The John Frum movement of Tanna emerged around the late 1930s; during the Second World War, the large quantities of supplies brought by the U.S. military led believers to hold that an American named John Frum would bring wealth, while rejecting missionaries and colonial rule; believers still hold a commemorative parade every year on 15 February.

religion.background: The islands of Vanuatu originally worshipped ancestors and nature spirits, with tribal rituals closely tied to the land. From the mid-19th century Presbyterian, Anglican and other missionaries arrived in succession, and although early missionaries were repeatedly killed, Christianity gradually spread. During the Anglo-French joint rule of 1906-1980, Britain supported Protestantism and France supported Catholicism, so religious and language divisions overlapped. The presence of U.S. troops during the Second World War gave rise to "cargo cult" movements such as John Frum. Today Vanuatu's constitution is founded on Christian principles, but traditional customs are still greatly valued.

language.official: The official languages are Bislama, English and French.

ranking.name: Bislama
ranking.description: Bislama is an English-based pidgin that formed in the 19th century: at that time Vanuatuans came into contact with European traders in the sandalwood and sea-cucumber trades, and from the 1860s to the 1900s large numbers of islanders were recruited or kidnapped to work on sugar plantations in Queensland, Australia, and Fiji, bringing this common language back to the islands on their return. The name itself comes from the French "bêche-de-mer" (sea cucumber). Because the country has more than a hundred indigenous languages, Bislama became the inter-ethnic lingua franca, and it was made the national language after independence in 1980.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was the language used by the British side in administration and schools during the Anglo-French joint rule of 1906-1980, and after independence it became an official language together with French and Bislama. About 60 percent of schools teach in English, and it is in common use in government, business and tourism, but very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French was the language of administration and education on the French side during the joint rule, and Catholic schools also taught in French. At independence the French-speaking and English-speaking areas were politically opposed, and some figures in the French-speaking areas even supported a secession movement. About 40 percent of schools still teach in French today, but very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Vanuatu is one of the countries with the highest language density in the world, with more than 100 Austronesian languages among a population of about 300,000. The sandalwood and sea-cucumber trade of the 19th century and labor recruitment for plantations in Australia and Fiji gave rise to the English-based Bislama. From 1906 Britain and France ruled jointly, each running schools in English and French respectively, forming a dual education system. After independence in 1980, Bislama became the national language, an official language together with English and French.

ranking.name: Lap lap
ranking.description: Yam, taro, banana or cassava is grated into a paste, spread on banana leaves, topped with coconut milk and meat or fish, wrapped up and baked in an earth oven.
ranking.history: Lap lap is the national dish of Vanuatu, and cooking in an earth oven is a tradition brought by the Austronesian ancestors when they migrated into the Pacific. Yam, taro and banana were all early "canoe crops" brought by the first migrants and have long been staples on the islands of Vanuatu. Lap lap is made in large quantities at weddings, coming-of-age ceremonies and tribal rituals, and is also a common dish at Sunday and family meals, with methods and ingredients varying slightly from island to island.

ranking.name: Kava
ranking.description: The roots of the kava pepper plant are ground or chewed and mixed with water and strained into a murky brown drink; it tastes bitter and astringent and numbs the mouth and tongue and relaxes the body.
ranking.history: Kava has a history of thousands of years in Vanuatu, and many scholars believe that the kava plant was first domesticated in Vanuatu. Traditionally only men gather at dusk at the village "nakamal" (men's meeting ground) to drink it, using it in reconciliation rituals, weddings and tribal councils. Today the capital, Port Vila, has many kava bars, and the government regulates kava varieties and exports by law; it is an important cash crop and cultural symbol of Vanuatu.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: The coconut crab is the largest land-dwelling arthropod, feeds on coconuts, and when steamed or cooked in coconut milk has sweet meat with a rich coconut aroma.
ranking.history: The islands of northern Vanuatu are known for their abundance of coconut crabs, which were in the past a prized ingredient for islanders at festivals and when entertaining honored guests. With the development of tourism, coconut crab became a signature dish of Port Vila restaurants, leading to overharvesting and a marked decline in numbers. The Vanuatu government has therefore set catch size limits and closed seasons, and some islands also apply conservation measures, in the hope of sustaining this traditional resource.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: Taro is a starchy tuber that can be baked in an earth oven, boiled or made into lap lap, with a creamy texture, and is the main everyday source of starch.
ranking.history: When the Austronesian people of the Lapita culture arrived in Vanuatu about three thousand years ago, they brought crops such as taro, and islanders subsequently developed techniques of growing water taro on irrigated terraces. Taro and yam are important symbols of wealth in traditional Vanuatu society and are exchanged and given in large quantities at weddings, funerals and chiefly title-taking ceremonies. Today it is still the foundation of the daily diet of rural families.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large starchy fruit that can be roasted directly over a fire, boiled or stewed in coconut milk, with a texture between potato and bread.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is one of the crops that the Austronesian ancestors brought to the Pacific by canoe and is widely grown on the islands of Vanuatu. One breadfruit tree can bear fruit for decades and supply a great deal of food in the harvest season, and in the past islanders also fermented and buried breadfruit to cope with food shortages after cyclones. Today it is still an important seasonal staple of Vanuatu households, often cooked with fish or coconut milk.
